strengths: The paper addresses an important and relevant code-generation problem: producing RTL that is functionally correct, synthesizable, and efficient, rather than optimizing textual correctness alone.

Integrating compilation, simulation, synthesis, and PPA analysis into a gated reinforcement-learning loop is well motivated. The advantage-level normalization and curriculum weighting provide a coherent response to heterogeneous reward scales and evaluation costs.

The empirical scope is unusually broad: four 7B base models, VerilogEval and two RTLLM versions, component and training-stage ablations, comparisons with GRPO/DAPO, multiple PDK/tool configurations, and an additional large-design benchmark.

The reported functional gains are large and consistent across base models. Standard testbench-based benchmarks provide credible evidence that the full training pipeline improves functional RTL generation.
The paper is generally clear, and the algorithm, reward hierarchy, runtime analysis, limitations, prompt templates, and example outputs make the overall workflow understandable.
weaknesses: The PPA evaluation protocol has a consequential selection bias: Equation 21 averages only over tasks for which each model generated a functionally correct design. Because the successful-task set differs by model, PPA averages are not directly comparable and can omit difficult failures. Correctness and PPA should be combined under a common task set or failures should receive a defined penalty; per-task paired results and coverage should also be reported.

The evidence for controllable multi-objective optimization is incomplete. Power, area, and delay are evaluated under different preference prompts and the best candidate among several attempts is selected, so the radar plots do not demonstrate that a single design improves all objectives simultaneously. A cross-preference matrix, Pareto-front analysis, and comparison against ordinary sampling or reranking would be needed to establish preference following and learned trade-off control.

Important PPA measurement details are absent, including clock and timing constraints, switching-activity assumptions, power-analysis mode, corners, placement/routing settings, and treatment of failed or unconstrained designs. Consequently, the physical meaning and reproducibility of the reported power, delay, and EDAP values are difficult to assess despite the multi-tool sensitivity experiment.

The automatic training-data validation is potentially circular: GPT-5 receives both the natural-language specification and the existing Verilog output when generating a testbench, after which that same code is accepted if it passes the generated testbench. Such tests may encode the implementation's behavior rather than independently validate intended semantics. No manual audit, testbench-quality statistics, mutation testing, or other estimate of false acceptance is reported.

The experiments report no random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or run-to-run variance. This is particularly problematic for RL training and stochastic pass@k/best-of-k comparisons. Training-curve smoothing does not substitute for independent replications.

Reproducibility is not yet adequate for Findings: the manuscript says the artifact is or will be open source but provides no usable artifact location, and omits core values such as the exact preference vectors, w_func, EMA factor, reward-processing details, and several EDA configurations. Reliance on GPT-5 and commercial Design Compiler also requires clearer versions, prompts, and open alternatives.

The ablations leave major confounds unresolved. The very large improvement from SFT+CDPO is not compared against additional SFT on the same RL prompts, rejection sampling, or EDA-based best-of-n reranking under equal generation and tool budgets. Thus, the evidence does not isolate policy learning from extra data and inference-time candidate selection.

Training data are collected from online repositories, but benchmark exclusion is described only as strict filtering without a deduplication or contamination methodology. Given that Verilog benchmarks and reference implementations are commonly mirrored online, the substantial benchmark gains require a stronger leakage audit.

Several interpretations overreach the measurements: lower EDAP across tool settings does not by itself establish learned micro-architectural patterns, and the barrel-shifter example mainly replaces structural mux instances with behaviorally equivalent shift operators that ordinary synthesis already lowers. The paper supports promising empirical improvement, but not yet all of its mechanistic and state-of-the-art claims.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: jointly improving functional correctness, synthesizability, and hardware efficiency in Verilog generation using direct feedback from compilation, simulation, synthesis, and physical-design tools.

The proposed framework is technically coherent. Hierarchical gating avoids unnecessary EDA calls, while advantage-level reward normalization and curriculum weighting offer a plausible way to combine heterogeneous feedback signals.

The empirical section is broad, covering four 7B base models, VerilogEval and RTLLM benchmarks, component and training-stage ablations, alternative RL objectives, several PDK/tool configurations, runtime, and a larger-design benchmark.
weaknesses: The PPA evaluation is not soundly comparable across models. Equations 15–21 discard tasks for which a model produces no functionally correct candidate and average PPA only over each model's successful-task set. Models are therefore evaluated on different, model-dependent subsets; harder failures disappear rather than being penalized. Selecting the best of several candidates compounds this survivorship bias. Reporting pass@5 separately does not repair the headline claims of superior joint correctness and PPA.

The evidence does not establish controllable multi-objective optimization. Results pool scores obtained under different preference prompts and sometimes select the best metric among five attempts, but do not measure preference adherence, Pareto quality, target-versus-nontarget trade-offs, or performance on a common candidate/task set. Consequently, the claim that CDPO learns nuanced and user-controllable PPA trade-offs is substantially stronger than the presented evidence.

Training-data contamination is insufficiently addressed. The SFT corpus is collected from online Verilog repositories, while common RTL benchmarks are themselves derived from publicly available designs. Stating that benchmark cases were excluded is inadequate without repository provenance and exact/near-duplicate or semantic-overlap analysis. This concern is especially important given the exceptionally large functional gains.

Functional supervision may be weak or circular: GPT-5 generates testbenches from existing code, the stated template requires only at least ten tests, and filtering verifies code against those generated tests. There is no testbench-coverage analysis or independent validation showing that these rewards reliably capture the natural-language specification. The case study illustrates the problem: the generated barrel shifter ignores the specification's explicit mux2X1 structural requirement while being counted as successful based on I/O behavior.

The PPA methodology lacks essential information. Clock and timing constraints, switching-activity assumptions for power, tool and library versions, synthesis/place-and-route scripts, treatment of failed runs, and whether baseline outputs were regenerated under identical decoding and EDA settings are not adequately documented. Some comparisons appear to combine newly evaluated systems with literature results, making fairness difficult to assess.

No uncertainty is reported despite stochastic generation and RL training: there are no repeated training runs, random seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. RTLLM is small, and percentage improvements based on a single run and selected candidates are therefore not sufficiently reliable.

Reproducibility is presently inadequate. The paper promises that code and scripts will be released but provides no accessible artifact, model checkpoints, generated outputs, training data, split identifiers, or complete configuration. Important CDPO parameters—including curriculum initialization/EMA settings, reward weights, and the actual preference-vector values—are missing or underspecified.

The contribution is only indirectly connected to core computational linguistics: it is principally an EDA/code-generation systems paper. That does not make it out of scope, but the paper offers little analysis of language understanding, specification grounding, or reasoning behavior beyond aggregate code-generation metrics.

Overall, the approach is plausible and the functional results are potentially valuable, but the biased PPA aggregation, unresolved leakage risk, incomplete evaluation of preference control, and missing reproducibility materials prevent a sound Findings recommendation. These issues require substantial re-evaluation, though they appear addressable in a revised submission.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practically relevant limitation of LLM-based RTL generation: functional correctness alone is insufficient without synthesizability and competitive power, performance, and area (PPA). Integrating compilation, simulation, synthesis, and backend feedback into training is well motivated.

ChipSeek provides a coherent end-to-end framework. Hierarchical gating reduces unnecessary EDA calls, while component-wise advantage normalization, curriculum weighting, and prompt-conditioned PPA preferences offer reasonable mechanisms for handling sparse, differently scaled objectives.

The empirical results are broad and consistently favorable across four 7B base models, multiple established benchmarks, functional and PPA metrics, several PDK/tool configurations, and a larger-design evaluation. The reported gains are substantial rather than marginal.

The paper includes useful ablations of training stages, reward components, advantage aggregation, curriculum scheduling, and preference vectors. These generally support the claimed contributions, and comparisons with GRPO and DAPO provide relevant algorithmic context.

Implementation details are comparatively extensive, including model and dataset sizes, compute, major hyperparameters, EDA tools, generation settings, and evaluation formulas. The proposed use of open-source EDA components and stated code-release plan are positive for reproducibility.

The presentation is generally clear, with a helpful system overview, explicit reward definitions, pseudocode, runtime analysis, and qualitative examples. The work is relevant to computational linguistics through tool-grounded reinforcement learning and controllable code generation.
weaknesses: The validity of functional correctness is limited by automatically generated testbenches with as few as ten cases. Passing such tests is not equivalent to semantic equivalence, and validation against a single reference implementation does not establish adequate coverage. This is particularly consequential because PPA rewards are only meaningful for genuinely equivalent designs; formal equivalence checking or substantially stronger coverage is needed.

The PPA evaluation lacks several details necessary to interpret or reproduce the measurements, including clock and timing constraints, switching-activity assumptions, treatment of sequential latency and throughput, and the precise synthesis/place-and-route recipes. Large gains such as those reported for the pipelined 64-bit adder merit equivalence and latency-preservation analysis.

The aggregation in Equations 15–21 averages PPA only over tasks for which each model produces a valid design. Consequently, different models may be compared on different, model-dependent subsets of tasks, potentially favoring systems that succeed only on easier cases. A paired comparison on a common task set, together with coverage, would be more rigorous.

Statistical reliability is underdeveloped. The paper reports no independent training seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or per-task dispersion, despite relatively small RTL benchmarks and stochastic sampling. It is therefore difficult to distinguish robust improvements from seed or sampling effects.

Several experimental inconsistencies reduce confidence: Table 4 labels Pass@1 while its discussion describes pass@5; EDAP values for apparently related Qwen2.5-Coder evaluations differ across tables without a sufficiently clear explanation; and the fairness and tuning budget of the GRPO/DAPO comparison are not specified.

The qualitative barrel-shifter example is not strong evidence of learned optimization. Behavioral shifts and an explicit multiplexer hierarchy can synthesize to equivalent structures, and the generated solution also disregards the prompt's explicit mux2X1 construction request. Post-synthesis structural comparisons would be needed to substantiate the proposed interpretation.

Contamination control is asserted but not documented. Because training data come from online repositories and benchmark prompts can be derived from public RTL, the paper should describe code-level and semantic deduplication against all evaluation suites.

Reproducibility remains conditional on a future artifact release, and the construction of the 29,127-example SFT set and 8,453-example RL set is insufficiently specified. Exact source repositories, licenses, filtering thresholds, preference-vector templates/weights, software versions, random seeds, and generated testbenches should be released.

The underlying CDPO ingredients—per-objective normalization, scheduled auxiliary rewards, and preference-weighted objectives—are individually fairly incremental. The systems contribution is compelling, but the paper currently overstates the evidence that CDPO itself, rather than the additional data and EDA supervision, is the decisive source of improvement. Overall, I view the work as sound and promising enough for Findings, with a close but not yet fully convincing case for the main conference.
